title: Monolith vs Microservices: Quick Revision Handbook
summary: Night-before revision notes on choosing between monolith and microservices, drawing service boundaries with bounded contexts and business capabilities, giving each service its own data, and migrating safely with the strangler fig pattern.

chapters.title: Monolith vs Microservices: The Mental Model
points: Monolith: one deployable unit, one process, usually one database; modules call each other in-process
Microservices: small independently deployable services, each owning one business function and its data, talking over the network (HTTP/gRPC/events)
Monolith wins on simplicity: one deploy, local function calls, ACID transactions, easy debugging; it fits small teams and unclear domains
Microservices win on independent deploys, per-service scaling, team autonomy and fault isolation; the price is network failure, latency, and distributed data consistency
Modular monolith: one deployable with strict module boundaries; the usual best starting point, and the cheapest path to splitting later

chapters.title: Bounded Contexts and Business Capabilities
points: Bounded context (DDD): a boundary inside which a domain model and its terms have one consistent meaning
Same word, different models: 'Customer' in Billing (payment method, invoices) differs from 'Customer' in Shipping (address, delivery window)
Decompose by business capability (Orders, Payments, Inventory, Shipping), what the business does, not by technical layer (UI service, DB service)
Service size rule: a service should be owned by one team and changeable without coordinating releases with another
Context map relationships: Customer/Supplier, Shared Kernel, Anti-Corruption Layer (translates a legacy model so it does not leak in)

chapters.title: Database per Service and Data Consistency
points: Database per service: only the owning service touches its data; others go through its API or events, never its tables
Shared database couples services by schema: one column change breaks several teams and blocks independent deploys
No cross-service joins or ACID transactions: use API composition (query several services and merge) or CQRS read models
Saga: a chain of local transactions, each with a compensating action (e.g. refund payment if inventory reservation fails); choreography via events, or orchestration via a coordinator
Eventual consistency: replicate data by events; use the outbox pattern to write the DB change and event atomically, and make consumers idempotent

chapters.title: Strangler Fig Migration
points: Strangler fig: put a facade (API gateway or reverse proxy) in front of the monolith and route traffic to new services one capability at a time
Steps: identify a seam, build the new service, route a slice of traffic to it, verify, retire the old code; repeat
Pick the first slice with low coupling and clear value (e.g. notifications, search); leave the tangled core for last
Keep data in sync during transition: dual writes are risky, prefer change data capture or an anti-corruption layer; migrate data ownership last
Rollback is just re-pointing the route, which is the main advantage over a big-bang rewrite

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Trade-offs
points: Distributed monolith: services that must deploy together or share a database get all the cost of microservices and none of the benefit
Splitting too early: boundaries guessed before the domain is understood are wrong and expensive to move; start with a modular monolith
Nano-services and chatty calls: a request needing many synchronous hops multiplies latency and failure rate; prefer coarser services or async events
Missing operational basics: without tracing, centralised logs, CI/CD per service and timeouts/retries/circuit breakers, microservices are undebuggable
Team fit (Conway's Law): architecture mirrors team structure; few engineers means a monolith is usually right

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Monolith vs Microservices
points: Default path: modular monolith, extract a service only when a clear pain exists (scaling, team conflict, deploy cadence)
Boundary test: one team, one capability, one bounded context, one data store
Data rules: own your data, no shared tables, no cross-service joins; use APIs, events, sagas, outbox
Migration recipe: facade, new service, route slice, verify, retire old code, data ownership last
Red flags: lockstep deploys, shared DB, chatty sync chains, no tracing, more services than engineers
